KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) -- Nepal's government ordered the country's army chief of staff fired Sunday, touching off street protests and a split in Nepal's Maoist-dominated ruling coalition. General Rookmangud Katawal gestures after inspecting the guard of honour in New Delhi on December 12, 2007. But Gen. Nepal's Cabinet voted to dismiss Katawal after the military refused the government's order to stop recruiting about 3,000 new soldiers to fill vacant positions when it has yet to take in former Maoist rebels, as a 2006 peace deal required. The move prompted the Maoists' largest coalition partner to quit the government, the party's leader said. "Without consensus, the ongoing peace process will not reach its logical conclusion and the drafting of the new constitution will not be possible," said Ishwor Pokharel, general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist). "The consensus that existed so far has come to standstill." Supporters of both sides in the dispute took to the streets for demonstrations Sunday. Despite sporadic clashes between the two factions, there were no serious injuries reported. The Maoists laid down their arms and won power in 2008 elections after an agreement that ended a decade-long insurgency. Under the deal, more than 19,000 former insurgents were to be integrated into the country's security forces. But two weeks ago, the government asked Katawal to explain why he went to the Supreme Court to challenge the government's refusal to extend the tenure of eight brigadier generals in March. Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that the government was not satisfied with Katawal's explanation and fired him -- three months before his scheduled retirement -- in a meeting that the Maoists' coalition partners boycotted. Pokharel said his party urged the Maoists not to fire Katawal without a consensus in the country's parliament. He said the Maoists, led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, ignored that advice. "We do not like the way the Maoists' way of functioning," Pokharel said. The Maoists hold 238 of the 601 seats in parliament, while Pokharel's party has 109. The Maoists could continue to hold power with the support of smaller parties, but Pokharel said his party is working to form a new ruling coalition. The Cabinet named an interim army chief, but presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal told CNN that 18 parties in Nepal's parliament asked Yadav to keep Katawal on the job. There was no immediate reaction from the government on the president's decision.

KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) -- On Sunday, Nepal's government issued an order to remove the nation's army chief of staff, a decision that sparked demonstrations in the streets and fractured the Maoist-led governing coalition.

However, General Rookmangud Katawal has declined to step down, and according to a presidential spokesman, President Ram Baran Yadav -- who serves as the constitutional supreme commander of Nepal's military -- has instructed Katawal to keep his position.

The decision to remove Katawal came after Nepal's Cabinet held a vote, prompted by the military's defiance of a government directive. The government had ordered the army to halt its recruitment of roughly 3,000 new personnel meant to fill empty posts, arguing that former Maoist fighters had not yet been absorbed into the ranks as mandated by a peace accord signed in 2006.

This action led the biggest party allied with the Maoists to withdraw from the government, according to that party's leader.

"The peace process currently under way cannot reach its rightful end without agreement, and it will be impossible to draft the new constitution," stated Ishwor Pokharel, who serves as general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist). "The agreement that had held until now has ground to a halt."

On Sunday, backers from both sides of the conflict gathered in the streets to protest. Although occasional confrontations broke out between the rival groups, no significant injuries were reported.

In 2008, following a pact that brought an end to a ten-year uprising, the Maoists surrendered their weapons and secured victory in the elections. That agreement stipulated that upwards of 19,000 ex-rebels would be brought into Nepal's security forces.

Two weeks earlier, though, the government had demanded that Katawal justify his decision to take the matter to the Supreme Court. He had challenged the government's March refusal to prolong the terms of eight brigadier generals.

Krishna Bahadur Mahara, a government spokesman, stated on Sunday that officials found Katawal's justification unsatisfactory and dismissed him just three months ahead of his planned retirement. The Maoists' coalition allies stayed away from the meeting where this occurred.

Pokharel explained that his party had advised the Maoists against removing Katawal unless parliament reached a consensus. He added that the Maoists, headed by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, disregarded this counsel.

"We are not pleased with how the Maoists conduct their affairs," Pokharel remarked.

Of the 601 parliamentary seats, the Maoists control 238, whereas Pokharel's party occupies 109. While the Maoists might retain power by relying on backing from smaller parties, Pokharel indicated that his party is actively trying to build a new governing alliance.

Although the Cabinet appointed a temporary army chief, presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal informed CNN that 18 political parties within Nepal's parliament had requested that Yadav allow Katawal to remain in his role. The government offered no immediate response to the president's move.

# Political Crisis in Nepal: The Dismissal of General Katawal

Nepal's political landscape was thrown into turmoil when the Maoist-dominated government made the controversial decision to dismiss the country's army chief, General Rookmangud Katawal. The move came amid escalating tensions between the civilian government and the military leadership over several contentious issues.

## The Roots of the Conflict

At the heart of the dispute were fundamental disagreements about how to handle military recruitment practices and, more significantly, the integration of former Maoist rebel fighters into the national army. This integration was a key requirement outlined in the 2006 peace agreement, which had officially ended a decade-long civil war that had claimed thousands of lives. The Maoists, who had transitioned from an armed insurgency to a political party, insisted that their former combatants be absorbed into the national security forces as promised. General Katawal, however, resisted these efforts, creating a direct confrontation between the army establishment and the elected government.

## A Constitutional Standoff

When the government voted to remove General Katawal from his position, the general refused to comply with the order and declined to step down. He received crucial backing from the country's president, who supported his position against the Maoist-led administration. This created a serious constitutional crisis, pitting the executive government against both the military and the presidency, and exposing deep divisions within Nepal's fragile post-war power structure.

## Consequences and Fallout

The attempted dismissal had immediate and far-reaching repercussions. Street protests erupted as supporters and opponents of the decision took to the streets, reflecting the polarized state of Nepali politics. The crisis also destabilized the governing coalition itself: the largest partner in the coalition withdrew its support, effectively pulling out of the government in protest over the handling of the situation.

## Threats to Peace and Democracy

The unfolding events posed a grave threat to Nepal's hard-won peace process. The delicate balance that had been established following the end of the civil war appeared to be unraveling, raising fears of renewed instability. Perhaps most critically, the crisis jeopardized the ongoing efforts to draft Nepal's new constitution—a foundational document meant to solidify the country's transition to a stable, democratic republic. With the political consensus shattered, the future of both the peace agreement and the constitutional process hung in the balance.

# Constitutional Crisis: Nepal's Civilian-Military Standoff of 2009

## Background

In May 2009, Nepal faced one of its most serious political crises since the end of its decade-long civil war, as a confrontation erupted between the Maoist-led government and the country's army chief, General Rookmangud Katawal. The dispute ultimately led to the resignation of Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, widely known as "Prachanda."

## The Central Dispute

The conflict centered on the government's attempt to dismiss General Katawal, the Chief of Army Staff. Several interconnected issues drove the tensions:

**Integration of Former Combatants:** A key sticking point involved the integration of former Maoist fighters (People's Liberation Army) into the Nepal Army. This integration was a component of the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement that ended the civil war. General Katawal reportedly resisted the wholesale absorption of former rebel combatants into the national army.

**Recruitment Dispute:** The army had continued recruiting new soldiers despite government objections, arguing it was replacing retiring personnel. The Maoists viewed this as defiance of civilian authority.

**Sports Controversy:** Tensions were exacerbated by the army's refusal to participate in a national games event that included Maoist combatants.

## The Crisis Unfolds

On May 3, 2009, Prime Minister Prachanda's government moved to sack General Katawal, asserting civilian control over the military. However, the decision immediately sparked a constitutional confrontation.

President Ram Baran Yadav, of the Nepali Congress party, intervened by writing to General Katawal, requesting that he remain in his position. The President's action effectively countermanded the government's decision, creating a direct clash between the executive branches.

## Political Fallout

The dispute exposed deep divisions within Nepal's coalition government. The Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), a key coalition partner, withdrew its support over the handling of the army chief's dismissal, leaving the Maoist government without a working majority.

Facing this political impasse, Prime Minister Prachanda resigned on May 4, 2009, after approximately eight months in office. In his resignation address, he characterized the President's intervention as unconstitutional and framed the crisis as a matter of protecting civilian supremacy over the military and safeguarding the peace process.

## Broader Significance

The crisis highlighted several fundamental challenges facing Nepal during its post-conflict transition:

- **Civil-Military Relations:** The dispute raised questions about the balance of power between elected civilian authorities and military institutions.

- **Peace Process Fragility:** The confrontation underscored the difficulties in implementing the peace agreement, particularly regarding combatant integration.

- **Constitutional Ambiguity:** The clash between the Prime Minister and President revealed uncertainties in the roles and powers defined under Nepal's interim constitution, as the country was still in the process of drafting a new permanent constitution.

## Aftermath

Following Prachanda's resignation, Madhav Kumar Nepal of the CPN (UML) formed a new coalition government. General Katawal remained in his position and eventually retired at the scheduled end of his tenure later in 2009.

The episode left lasting political tensions and complicated the ongoing peace process and constitution-drafting efforts, contributing to years of political instability that would characterize Nepalese politics in the following period.

# Nepal Political Crisis Deepens as Standoff Over Army Chief Threatens Fragile Peace Process

**KATHMANDU, Nepal** — Nepal's fledgling democracy faced one of its gravest tests as a bitter standoff between the Maoist-led government and the country's army chief escalated into a full-blown political crisis, threatening to unravel the peace process that ended a decade-long civil war.

## The Flashpoint

At the center of the confrontation is General Rookmangud Katawal, the chief of the Nepal Army, whom the Maoist-led government moved to dismiss over accusations of insubordination. The government cited several grievances, including the army's refusal to halt recruitment of new soldiers and its reluctance to integrate former Maoist combatants into the national force.

The Maoists, who won the largest bloc in the 2008 Constituent Assembly elections following their transition from insurgency to mainstream politics, accused Katawal of defying civilian authority and undermining the elected government's mandate.

## Presidential Intervention

The crisis intensified when President Ram Baran Yadav, in an unprecedented move, intervened to reinstate General Katawal shortly after the government announced his dismissal. The president's action set up a direct constitutional confrontation between the office of the head of state and the executive government led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, widely known by his nom de guerre "Prachanda."

Maoist leaders denounced the presidential intervention as unconstitutional, arguing it exceeded the ceremonial powers granted to the head of state and represented dangerous interference in civilian governance.

## The Integration Question

The dispute over Katawal is deeply entangled with one of the most sensitive issues of Nepal's peace process: the fate of some 19,000 former Maoist fighters confined to United Nations-monitored cantonments since the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement.

The Maoists have long demanded that their combatants be integrated into the national army — a proposal fiercely resisted by the military establishment and opposition parties, who fear the "politicization" of Nepal's armed forces. Critics worry that absorbing former rebels could compromise the army's neutrality, while Maoists insist integration is essential to fulfilling the peace accord's promises.

The army's continued recruitment drive, which the government said violated the spirit of the peace agreement, became a symbol of this broader deadlock.

## Political Fallout

The crisis exposed deep fractures within Nepal's coalition government. The Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), or UML, a key coalition partner, withdrew its support from the government over the handling of the army chief's dismissal, leaving the Maoist administration's future in serious doubt.

**Reactions from across the political spectrum reflected the nation's polarization:**

The **Nepali Congress**, the main opposition party, condemned the government's move against Katawal, characterizing it as an authoritarian overreach that threatened democratic institutions and civilian-military balance.

The **UML** leadership expressed alarm over what it described as the Maoists' unilateral decision-making and their failure to build consensus among coalition partners on such a consequential matter.

**Maoist leaders**, for their part, framed the standoff as a struggle between the forces of change and entrenched conservative interests seeking to preserve the old order. Prachanda's party argued that civilian supremacy over the military was a fundamental principle of the new republic.

## International Concern

The turmoil drew close attention from Nepal's neighbors and the international community. India, which shares deep historical and strategic ties with Nepal, monitored developments carefully, as did other regional stakeholders concerned about stability in the Himalayan nation. United Nations officials overseeing the peace process urged all parties to exercise restraint and preserve the hard-won gains of the accord.

## A Peace Process at Risk

Analysts warned that the confrontation risked derailing Nepal's transition from monarchy to republic — a transformation formalized in 2008 when the Constituent Assembly abolished the 240-year-old monarchy and declared the country a federal democratic republic.

The Constituent Assembly, tasked with drafting a new constitution, found its work overshadowed by the political drama, raising fears of delays to the crucial constitution-writing process.

"This is a defining moment for Nepal's democracy," one political observer in Kathmandu noted. "How the country resolves the tension between civilian authority and military independence will shape its institutions for years to come."

## Looking Ahead

As Nepal navigated the uncertain path forward, the central questions remained unresolved: Could the fragile coalition survive? Would the integration of former combatants proceed? And could the country's nascent institutions withstand the strain of competing claims to power?

For a nation still healing from a conflict that claimed more than 13,000 lives, the stakes could hardly be higher. The resolution of the Katawal standoff would test whether Nepal's diverse political forces could reconcile their differences through democratic means — or whether the promise of the peace process might slip away.

*This is a developing story.*
